summary: Gives an overview of telephone number portability in the Global Switched Telephone Network, where users keep their numbers when changing providers. This turns a dialed number from a physical routing address into a virtual one, requiring translation before calls can be routed.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3482 explains how a call reaches a telephone number whose provider has changed. The number becomes a lookup key rather than an address: the network asks a portability database for a routing number and sends the call there. The document describes the four schemes used to do that, the databases and signalling involved, and what IP telephony has to carry to work with them.

subtitle: How telephone numbers are looked up so a call reaches the provider that now serves the line

tldr.problem: A geographic telephone number was designed as a routing address, so moving a line to another provider meant moving the number as well. Regulators wanted subscribers to keep their numbers when they changed provider, which turned every number into a lookup rather than an address.
tldr.mechanism: The network asks a Number Portability Database for a routing number and uses that to route the call. Four schemes are described: All Call Query, Query on Release, Call Dropback and Onward Routing, differing in how much work the donor network does and which database is consulted.
tldr.outcome: The document gives the IETF's IP telephony work the vocabulary and the signalling details it needs to interwork with the telephone network, including how the routing number travels in ISUP and in SIP.

today: RFC 3482 is an Informational memo published in February 2003, and the unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is an overview rather than a specification: it describes how number portability worked in the telephone network so that the IETF's IP telephony work could interwork with it.

sections.title: Why Numbers Had to Become Portable
sections.content:
RFC 3482 gives an overview of E.164 telephone number portability in the Global Switched Telephone Network, the GSTN. Number portability is a regulatory imperative in many countries, seeking to liberalise local telephony service competition by enabling subscribers to retain their telephone numbers while changing service providers.

Geographic E.164 numbers were intentionally designed as hierarchical routing addresses. They could be analysed digit by digit to ascertain the country, the serving network provider, the serving end-office switch and the specific line of the called party. Without portability, a subscriber wishing to change service providers would incur a number change, because the number pointed at the switch that served it before. The cost and inconvenience to the subscriber is seen as a barrier to competition.

Portability changes the fundamental nature of a dialled number, from a hierarchical physical routing address to a virtual address, and the network must translate the latter into the former. The document compares this with network address translation in IP, which contains the address change at the edge of the network and lets the core keep using address blocks that can be aggregated.

Portability also splits the historical role of a subscriber's number into two or more data elements, a dialled virtual address and a network routing address, which must be made available to network elements through an NP translation database, carried by forward call signalling, and recorded on call detail records.
sections.plainLanguage: Before portability, a telephone number was also the address of the switch that served the line, so moving to another provider meant moving your number too. Portability makes the number a lookup key instead: the network asks a database where the line is now and routes the call there.

sections.title: Three Kinds of Portability
sections.content:
Three kinds of portability are distinguished. Service provider portability, the subject of the document, is the ability to change service provider while keeping the same phone number, also known as operator portability. Location portability is the ability to change the subscriber's fixed service location while keeping the same number. Service portability is the ability to change the subscribed services, for example from plain old telephone service to Integrated Services Digital Network services, while keeping the same number.

Numbers themselves are also split. Non-geographic numbers, commonly used for service-specific applications such as freephone numbers beginning 800 or 0800, do not reveal the location of the number, and their portability is called non-geographic number portability. Geographic number portability covers traditional fixed or wireline numbers and also mobile numbers that are allocated out of geographic number range prefixes; in the United States the same thing is called local number portability. Mobile number portability refers to portability in mobile networks, and where local and mobile portability interwork, a subscriber can keep the number across fixed and mobile service types.

Three networks have roles in the schemes. The donor network is the network that first assigned the telephone number, out of a number range administratively assigned to it. The new serving network is the network that currently serves the ported number, and the old serving network is the network that served it before. Because a number can be ported several times, the old serving network is not necessarily the donor network, but the donor network stays the same for any given number.

The document also distinguishes interim portability, which uses remote call forwarding-like measures to forward calls to ported numbers through the donor network to the new service network, from true portability, which seeks to remove the donor network from the call or signalling path altogether. The distinction is often a national regulatory matter.
sections.plainLanguage: The document names three kinds of portability: changing provider, changing location, and changing the kind of service. It also names the three networks involved: the donor network that first held the number, the network that used to serve it, and the network that serves it now.

sections.title: Four Ways to Find the New Network
sections.content:
Four schemes support service provider portability for geographic numbers. They all assume the same three networks, and the port itself has already happened before the call arrives.

  • All Call Query (ACQ). The originating network receives the call and sends a query to a centrally administered Number Portability Database, a copy of which usually resides on a network element in its network or is reached through a third party provider. The database returns the routing number associated with the dialled directory number, and the originating network uses it to route the call to the new serving network.
  • Query on Release (QoR). The originating network routes the call to the donor network, which releases the call and indicates that the dialled number has been ported out of its switch. The originating network then sends a query to its copy of the central database, receives the routing number, and routes the call to the new serving network.
  • Call Dropback. The originating network routes the call to the donor network, which detects that the number has been ported out and checks with its own internal network-specific database. That database returns the routing number, and the donor network releases the call by providing the routing number, so the originating network can route the call to the new serving network. This scheme is also known as Return to Pivot.
  • Onward Routing (OR). The first steps are as in dropback, but the donor network uses the routing number to route the call to the new serving network itself.

The comparison is sharp. Only ACQ leaves the donor network out of the routing of the call to the new serving network, and it is the most efficient in terms of using switching and transmission facilities. Only OR sets up two physical call segments, one from the originating network to the donor network and the other from the donor network to the new serving network, which makes it the least efficient. QoR and dropback set up calls to the donor network first but release the call back to the originating network, which then initiates a new call to the current serving network, with circuits reserved and released one by one.

ACQ and QoR use centralized databases that hold ported number information from multiple networks. Dropback and OR use an internal database in the donor network that holds only information about the numbers ported out of that network, and it can even sit on the donor switch itself, in which case no query to a stand-alone database is needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Four schemes find the new network for a ported number. The difference is how much work the donor network does: in one scheme it is left out of the call entirely, in one it takes over the call, and in two it answers a query and hands the call back.

sections.title: Querying the Portability Database
sections.content:
The ACQ and QoR schemes require a switch to query the database for routing information, and various standards have been defined for the switch-to-database interface. The query contains the dialled directory number and the response contains the routing number.

In the United States and Canada five interfaces are listed. Advanced Intelligent Network using the ANSI version of the Intelligent Network Application Part, carried over ANSI Message Transfer Part levels 1 to 3, ANSI SCCP and ANSI TCAP, which is modelled on the Public Office Dialing Plan trigger in the AIN 0.1 call model. The Intelligent Network interface, similar to the one used for querying the 800 databases, over the same stack. ANSI IS-41 over the same stack, for the IS-41 based cellular and PCS wireless switches. Global System for Mobile Communication Mobile Application Part, for PCS1900 wireless switches based on GSM technologies. And ISUP triggerless translation, where the translation is performed transparently to the switching network by the signalling network: the Initial Address Message is examined to see whether the Called Party Number has already been translated and, if not, an NPDB query is performed and the message parameters are modified to reflect the result before it is forwarded on to the designated point code.

In Europe there are two interfaces, Capability Set 1 and Capability Set 2 of the ITU-TS INAP, carried over ITU-TS MTP levels 1 to 3, ITU-TS SCCP and ITU-TS TCAP. All the European implementations so far are based on CS1. In most, if not all, cases in Europe, calls to wireless directory numbers are routed to the wireless donor network first, where an internal database is queried to determine whether the number has been ported out, and the interface to that internal database is not subject to standardization.
sections.plainLanguage: Where the network asks the database for a routing number, it needs a standard way to ask. North America has five such interfaces and Europe has two, each sitting on a stack of signalling protocols. In Europe, calls to mobile numbers usually go to the old network first, which looks them up locally.

sections.title: Carrying the Routing Number in the Signalling
sections.content:
In the United States and Canada, a ten-digit North American Numbering Plan number called the Location Routing Number is assigned to every switch involved in portability. A switch is not reachable unless it has a unique number range assigned to it, so the LRN for a switch always comes out of a code assigned to that switch. The LRN of the switch currently serving a ported number is what the database returns as the routing number, and the approach is often called the LRN scheme or method. The LRN is a non-dialable address, because the same ten-digit value may also be assigned to a line on that switch, and a switch may have more than one LRN.

When a switch formulates the ISUP Initial Address Message for the next switch, it puts the ten-digit LRN in the Called Party Number parameter and the originally dialled directory number in the Generic Address Parameter, with a new code in that parameter indicating that it holds the dialled number. It also sets a new bit in the Forward Call Indicator, the Ported Number Translation Indicator, to imply that the database query has already been performed, so switches downstream do not query again. When the terminating switch sees that bit and finds its own LRN in the Called Party Number, it retrieves the dialled number from the Generic Address Parameter and terminates the call. A dialled number in a portable code does not mean that a number has been ported, because the databases hold no records for numbers that have not moved; in that case the database returns the dialled number itself, and the switch sets the indicator but keeps the dialled number in place.

In some European countries a routing number is prefixed to the dialled directory number instead. The United Kingdom uses prefixes of the form 5XXXXX and Italy uses C600XXXXX. The prefix can identify the serving network, which needs another query to the internal database at that network to find the serving switch, or it can identify the serving switch directly, which needs no extra query. Three methods carry the directory number and the routing number in the Initial Address Message: two separate parameters, with the routing number in the Called Party Number and the dialled number in a new Called Directory Number parameter; two separate parameters, with the dialled number in the Called Party Number and the routing number in a new Network Routing Number parameter; or one concatenated parameter holding the routing number plus the dialled number. The first and third use a new value of the Nature of Address indicator to say which arrangement applies, for example 126 in Spain and 112 in Denmark. A further option is a Number Portability Forwarding Information parameter with a four-bit status indicator that says whether a query was done and whether the number is ported. All of these enhancements can only be used in the country that defined them, because portability is supported within a nation and the coding is usually not passed across national boundaries unless interconnection agreements allow it.
sections.plainLanguage: The routing number has to travel with the call. In North America it is a ten-digit Location Routing Number that replaces the dialled number in the signalling, while the dialled number is kept in another field. In Europe it is a prefix added in front of the dialled number. Each country has its own way of doing this.

sections.title: What This Means for IP Telephony
sections.content:
The document names three areas of impact on IP telephony work in the IETF: interoperation between portability in the telephone network and IP telephony, portability implemented or emulated inside IP telephony, and interconnection to the portability administrative environment.

Querying the existing national databases from an IP network would be an impractical job, because there are several interface standards with different protocol stacks and national variations. The document suggests alternatives: using IP entities that behave like the international switches of the telephone network and query the databases of the terminating country, defining a common interface that all the databases support, with ENUM, LDAP and SIP named as candidates, or using an interworking function to convert from one protocol to another.

For calls between two telephone networks that travel over IP, SIP has to carry three pieces of portability information: the called directory number, a routing number, and an indicator that the database query has already been done, so that the terminating network does not query again. When the routing number is present, it is the routing number, not the called directory number, that should be used for routing decisions. The SIP URL is one mechanism for carrying this, and an extension to the tel URL is described as a better choice, carried as optional parameters in the user portion of the sip URL. The document also warns that the entities retrieving portability information must collect the complete called directory number before retrieving it, otherwise the retrieval will not succeed, which matters where overlap signalling is involved. It recommends that carriers use a different domain tree for their own ENUM records than the one used for subscribers, so that a subscriber who changes provider does not leave stale records behind.

The security section adds a warning for networks that launch these queries from softswitches, media gateway controllers or call managers over the Internet, rather than over the closed SS7 signalling network. If the routing number or routing prefix in a response is altered during transport, the call is routed to the wrong place, so the document recommends that the queries be transported via a secure transport layer or with added security mechanisms to ensure data integrity.
sections.plainLanguage: For networks built on IP, the hard part is reaching the telephone network's databases, because every country uses different interfaces. The document suggests routing the lookups through a few IP entities that speak the national interfaces, and carrying the routing number and the dialled number in the SIP signalling.
